article.title: IBM Releases Granite TimeSeries PatchTST-FM-r2, a Time Series Forecasting Model Topping GIFT-Eval Among Open Models
article.summary: IBM Research released an open-weight time series forecasting model it says ranks first among permissively licensed models on the GIFT-Eval leaderboard.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

IBM Research has released Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2, an open-weight forecasting model that the company says is, as of early September 2026, "the top performing zero-shot model released under a permissive, commercial-friendly open-source license" among replicable zero-shot entries on the GIFT-Eval leaderboard, according to [IBM Research's announcement on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/ibm-releases-sota-granite-time-series).

## What We Know

The model combines "an updated architecture, a larger pretraining corpus, probabilistic forecasting, support for imputation of missing values" in a roughly 385-million-parameter model, according to the [Hugging Face blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/ibm-releases-sota-granite-time-series). The [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-patchtst-fm-r2) independently confirms the parameter count and adds that the model uses a hidden dimension of 1024.

On the GIFT-Eval benchmark, IBM Research reports that PatchTST-FM-r2 "achieves a geometric-mean CRPS of 0.467, placing it immediately behind TimesFM-3" while ranking first among models released under permissive licenses, according to the [Hugging Face blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/ibm-releases-sota-granite-time-series). When the comparison is widened to include models that were allowed to train on benchmark data, the same post says PatchTST-FM-r2 ranks "3rd for CRPS and 4th for MASE" and "outperforms several pretrained models, including Chronos-2, Timer-S1, and Toto variants." The [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-patchtst-fm-r2) corroborates the broader-comparison ranking, stating the model "ranks 3rd and 4th in CRPS and MASE, respectively" when pretrained models are included.

Architecturally, the model "retains the patch-based representation" of its predecessor but adds "conformer layers" that combine "multi-head self-attention with temporal convolution," per the [Hugging Face blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/ibm-releases-sota-granite-time-series). The [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-patchtst-fm-r2) details this further, describing "a convolution layer after the multi-head self-attention (MHSA) layer" inside each conformer block, overlapping patches of size 16 with a stride of 8, and a pre-head layer norm added for training stability. The number of transformer blocks was expanded from 20 in the prior PatchTST-FM-r1 release to 30 in r2, according to the model card. The model supports context lengths of up to 8,192 steps and predicts 99 quantiles, a detail confirmed by both the blog post and the model card.

Training data came from four sources, per the [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-patchtst-fm-r2): a selected subset of the GiftEvalPretrain datasets, synthetic data generated with KernelSynth, a TSMixup dataset built "based on the same process described in the Chronos paper," and an in-house CauKer dataset of roughly 500,000 generated sequences.

IBM is releasing the model as "a state-of-the-art zero-shot time series foundation model," in the model card's own description, and is dual-licensing it "under the OpenMDW License version 1.0 and the Apache License 2.0," letting users pick either license. OpenMDW is the Linux Foundation- and PyTorch Foundation-developed license aimed at covering model weights, architecture, and documentation under a single permissive grant; as [previously reported](/article/2026-08/24-linux-foundation-asks-osi-to-approve-openmdw-11-ai-model-license-as-reviewers-split-over-its-copyright-termination-clause), IBM was already named among the license's early adopters when the Linux Foundation submitted an updated version, OpenMDW-1.1, to the Open Source Initiative for formal approval in August.

The model card cites an accompanying paper, ["Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06909), as the basis for the architecture work behind the release.

## What We Don't Know

The two IBM-published sources give slightly different snapshot dates for the GIFT-Eval standings underlying these rankings — the blog post cites results "as of September 8, 2026" while the model card cites results "as of August 31, 2026" — so the leaderboard position could shift as new entries are submitted. Neither source discloses inference latency, hardware requirements, or pricing for any hosted version of the model, and neither describes specific enterprise products that will incorporate it.
